statement: In three randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies of healthy adults with previous MDMA experience, a second dose taken 2 or 24 hours after the first raised plasma concentrations by more than the dose alone would predict, but did not raise the peak of the effects people felt. After a second 100 mg dose 24 hours later, exposure was 77% higher and peak concentration 29% higher than after the first dose, while pupil diameter, extraocular balance, one questionnaire subscale and prolactin did not change at all and the other effects rose only slightly (Farre et al., 2004). After 50 mg followed by 100 mg two hours later, peak concentration was about half as high again as after 100 mg alone (311 against 203 ng/mL), 12.8% above dose proportionality, yet heart rate did not rise in peak or area under the curve and none of the wanted subjective effects (euphoria, liking, stimulation) differed, while blood pressure, temperature and pupil diameter did rise (Peiro et al., 2013). In the largest and only registered study, a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg raised peak concentration 1.5-fold and lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour (5.6 hours, SD 1.8, against 4.6, SD 1.5) without raising peak ratings (83 against 85 for 'any drug effect'; 86 against 87 for 'good drug effect') or peak blood pressure, heart rate or temperature (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026). The studies read this as acute tolerance; in all three, effects subsided while plasma concentrations were still high. None of them modelled the relation between concentration and effect, so 'less than expected' is a judgement against dose proportionality, and the peak ratings in the booster study were already above 80 out of 100, where a rating cannot rise much further. All used 50 to 180 mg of known, pure MDMA in a quiet laboratory in 9, 10 and 23 people, two of the three studies in men only; no study has given more than two doses.
plain: If you take a second dose within a few hours or a day, the drug level in your blood goes up by more than the extra dose alone explains, because MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. The effects do not rise to match. In three laboratory studies the strongest feeling was no stronger after the second dose; what changed was how long it lasted, about an hour more. Heart rate did not rise further either, while blood pressure and body temperature did. The studies were small (9, 10 and 23 people), used pure MDMA in a quiet room, and none of them gave more than two doses.
population: Healthy adults with previous recreational MDMA experience in laboratory studies (9 men, 10 men, and 23 people of whom 11 were women), screened to exclude medical and psychiatric illness; two studies included only people who metabolize MDMA quickly
exposure: A second dose of MDMA taken 2 or 24 hours after the first (study conditions: 100 mg then 100 mg 24 hours apart; 50 mg then 100 mg 2 hours apart; 120 mg then 60 mg 2 hours apart)
comparator: The same people taking a single dose or placebo in a separate session, and their own first dose
outcome: Peak and duration of subjective effects, heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, pupil diameter, and plasma concentrations of MDMA and its metabolites
magnitude: Twenty-four-hour interval: exposure 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) after the second 100 mg dose against 1452 (SD 771) after the first, a ratio of 1.77; peak 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), ratio 1.29 (both p<=0.001); peak systolic pressure rise 34 mm Hg against 25 and diastolic 20 against 10; pupil diameter, Maddox-wing, the amphetamine subscale and prolactin unchanged (Farre et al., 2004). Two-hour interval, 50 then 100 mg against 100 mg alone: peak concentration 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) against 202.92 (SD 30.30), p<0.001, which is 12.8% above dose proportionality, with exposure 16.2% above; heart-rate peak 33.05 (SD 13.25) against 33.50 (SD 11.87) beats/min and area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant; systolic area under the curve 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28), p=0.029; no significant difference in any wanted subjective effect (Peiro et al., 2013). Booster: peak concentration ratio 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and exposure ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); duration of 'any drug effect' 5.6 h (SD 1.8) against 4.6 (SD 1.5), p<0.01, with peak ratings 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20) and 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), not significant; half-life 7.2 h in both conditions (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026).

evidence.locator: Table 2, MDMA and MDA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first gave an area under the concentration-time curve of 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) against 1452 (SD 771) after the first, a ratio of 1.77 (77% higher), and a peak of 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), a ratio of 1.29 (29% higher), both p<=0.001; the metabolite MDA rose 64% in exposure and 40% at peak. About 12 ng/mL of MDMA from the first dose was still present when the second was given.

evidence.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraphs on physiological parameters (p. 367) and on hormones (p. 370); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (p. 373)
evidence.extracted: Effects after the second dose were slightly larger on blood pressure (peak systolic rise 34 mm Hg against 25; diastolic 20 against 10), heart rate (22 against 16 beats/min, significant only at 40 minutes) and cortisol (peak 49% higher), but unchanged on pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure, the amphetamine subscale and prolactin; the authors read the unchanged measures as 'the possible appearance of some degree of tolerance' and note that in no measure did effects exceed what the concentrations predicted.

evidence.locator: Table 1, HR and subjective rows (p. 887); Table 2, MDMA rows (p. 889); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 889)
evidence.extracted: Taking 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration to 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) from 202.92 (SD 30.30) with 100 mg alone (p<0.001), 12.8% above dose proportionality in peak and 16.2% in exposure, with half-life unchanged (10.48 h against 10.41). Heart rate did not rise with the added dose (peak 33.05, SD 13.25, against 33.50, SD 11.87; area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant), and none of the wanted subjective effects differed in peak or area under the curve.

evidence.locator: Table 1, SBP, DBP, T and PD rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 888)
evidence.extracted: In the same study the measures that did track concentration were blood pressure (systolic area under the curve 72.96, SD 22.12, against 49.35, SD 24.28, p=0.029; diastolic 46.82, SD 27.82, against 18.81, SD 21.09, p=0.015), pupil diameter (area under the curve 11.92, SD 3.33, against 9.42, SD 1.83, p=0.037) and body temperature (differences at 2.3, 2.6 and 3 hours), none of which differed significantly at the peak.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' and 'Good drug effect' rows; Table 3, MDMA rows
evidence.extracted: A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the duration of 'any drug effect' to 5.6 h (SD 1.8) from 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single dose (p<0.01) and raised the areas under several effect curves, while peak ratings did not differ (83, SD 21, against 85, SD 20 for 'any drug effect'; 86, SD 29, against 87, SD 19 for 'good drug effect'). Peak plasma concentration rose 1.50-fold (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and 9-hour exposure 1.47-fold (1.40-1.54), with half-life 7.2 h in both conditions.

Blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum; the authors attribute the unchanged maxima despite higher concentrations to acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that effects subsided within the 9-hour session while the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeded the mean peak after the single dose. The numerical autonomic values are in a supplement that the first reader did not open.

evidence.locator: Results > Participants and blinding, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Emax rows
evidence.extracted: Qualifications: blinding largely failed (every participant identified placebo correctly and 76% of MDMA sessions were identified correctly immediately afterwards), and the peak ratings against which the absence of an increase is measured were already 83-87 out of 100, so a ceiling on the scales cannot be separated from tolerance for the subjective measures.

risk_of_bias.note: All three are randomized or counterbalanced, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person studies with objective pharmacokinetics; but blinding failed in the one study that measured it, two of the three tested about forty outcomes without correction and tabulate only the significant ones, and one has no placebo-only session. Downgraded one level rather than two because the concentration findings and the autonomic measures do not depend on the blind.

inconsistency.note: Two independent groups at three intervals (2, 4 in a related study, and 24 hours) report the same pattern: concentrations above proportionality with effects that do not rise in step.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses, intervals and settings studied, and says so.

imprecision.note: Nine, ten and twenty-three participants; no confidence intervals for the differences in effect, and the pharmacokinetic ratios are the only estimates with intervals.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled within-person laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low. Status replicated: three studies from two independent groups, at different intervals and with different dose combinations, show the same dissociation between concentration and effect. The claim is worded as an observed dissociation; it does not state a size for the tolerance, because none of the studies fitted a concentration-effect model, and it names the ceiling of the rating scales as an alternative for the subjective peaks.

changelog.change: New draft claim from three full texts read in this round (Farre et al., 2004; Peiro et al., 2013; Humbert-Droz et al., 2026; cards sc_farre_2004, sc_peiro_2013, sc_humbert_droz_2026). Section 5 of the monograph template asks about tolerance on every page and MDMA had no such claim. Anchors ai-located by the first reader and not yet checked.
